cases.answer: The LeBlanc et al. case report (a 42-year-old man) used genetic testing and family history. The brain SPECT scan was read as most in keeping with Alzheimer's disease and not FTLD, and the MRI showed no specific pattern of atrophy. His father had bulbar ALS, which raised the possibility of a genetic FTD-ALS disorder. Genetic testing then found a GGGGCC repeat expansion in C9orf72, which confirmed the diagnosis. The authors say that although the neuroimaging findings were not consistent with FTD, the history led them to pursue genetic testing, which confirmed it. Post-mortem autopsy later showed FTLD with TDP pathology (type C).

Note: the DNA-editing paper in the folder is by Sachdeva et al. (PNAS 2024), which I take to be the 'Sachdev' in the question.

Liu et al. (2024), Cas13d RNA targeting:
- Endpoints were molecular only: poly-GP and poly-GA dipeptide repeat levels (ELISA) and reporter signals.
- In patient iPSCs, DPR knockdown was about 30–70%. In patient iPSC-derived motor neurons it was about 20–90%.
- In C9-500 BAC mice (AAV9 given at P0, tissue collected at 13 months), poly-GP and poly-GA fell and poly-GA inclusions decreased.
- Limits: in vitro, Cas13d cleavage fell as repeat length rose and it was nearly unable to degrade (GGGGCC)28. RNA foci were not reduced. Efficacy varied by line and cell type and correlated with Cas13d expression. The mice lack survival, motor and other behavioural or neurodegenerative phenotypes, so protective effects in patients 'require further evaluation'.

Sachdeva et al. (2024), DNA excision:
- Endpoints were C9orf72 transcript and protein levels, DPRs (poly-GA and poly-GP), nuclear TDP-43 loss, and electrophysiology (MEA and patch clamp). All were measured in motor neurons induced from isogenic iPSC lines.
- Excising the repeat expansion reverted these pathology readouts and improved electrophysiological function.
- Limits: the insights come mainly from edits in a single patient cell line, and the authors say replication in other patients and repeat lengths is needed. Silencing sense expression alone did not remove all DPRs. Excising the WT allele more than doubled poly-GP.

Why neither is an established human treatment: both studies are preclinical (cell lines, iPSC-derived neurons, and in Liu et al. a transgenic mouse with no disease phenotype). Neither reports any human treatment or clinical efficacy. The authors themselves call them proof-of-concept or note that further evaluation is needed.

cases.answer: No, that conclusion is not supported. Liu et al. (2024) did not report improved survival or motor function in C9-500 BAC mice. They note that this model has no survival or motor deficits. The outcomes measured were poly-GP and poly-GA levels and poly-GA inclusions, which fell after AAV9-Cas13d-S24 or -S30 treatment. C9orf72 transcripts, protein and RNA foci were unchanged. The authors state that, because current C9orf72 animal models lack behavioural phenotypes, protective effects still need evaluation.

cases.answer: In zebrafish embryos in Parameswaran et al. (2023), eif2ak2 (zebrafish PKR) knockdown with a morpholino rescued the antisense (C4G2)70 RNA phenotype but not the sense (G4C2)70 one. Co-injection of antisense (C4G2)70 RNA with the eif2ak2 splice-blocking morpholino significantly mitigated the abnormal axonal length and branching compared with a control morpholino. A translation-blocking morpholino also increased axonal length and ameliorated abnormal branching. No protective effect was seen when sense (G4C2)70 RNA was co-injected with the eif2ak2 splice-blocking morpholino. The authors conclude that PKR contributes to antisense but not sense repeat-RNA toxicity.

cases.answer:
Human frontal cortex: in post-mortem frontal cortex from C9FTD/ALS patients, phosphorylated PKR was increased by immunohistochemistry (especially in large pyramidal neurons, n = 4 per group). Phosphorylated eIF2α, normalised to total eIF2α, was also significantly increased by immunoblotting (6 controls vs 6 patients). The authors read this as activation of the PKR/eIF2α pathway in patients.

Patient-derived motor neurons: in two C9ORF72 patient-derived motor neuron lines and their isogenic controls, there were no differences in phosphorylated PKR or phosphorylated eIF2α at 38 days.

Interpretation: the authors suggest the PKR/eIF2α ISR pathway is possibly activated only at a later stage of disease pathogenesis. This explanation should be treated cautiously. It is speculative, as shown by the word 'possibly'. It rests on only two motor neuron lines at a single early culture age (38 days), and the study did not test late-stage motor neurons. Other explanations are not ruled out, such as the cell type (frontal cortex vs motor neurons) or differences between post-mortem tissue and cultured iPSC-derived cells.
